structure: eye diameter as percentage of head length
measurement: eye diameter 19.3–25.3% of head length (range in the species Description; eyes not reduced)
method: percentage range printed in the Description of a new species; the paper's Materials and methods print 'Most counts and morphometric measurements followed Tang et al. (2012), except for dorsal fin length (measured at the last simple dorsal ray) and caudal-peduncle depth (measured at the posterior anal-fin base), taken from the left side of the specimen.' and 'Measurements were made with digital calipers, and data were recorded to the nearest 0.1 mm.'; they do not define eye diameter or head length, so this is filed as sensory_anatomy (a ratio to head length), not eye_diameter_mm
conditions: Preserved type material of a new loach from Guangxi; the paper prints 'The species is known only from a karst cave' and says the specimens 'were obtained deep within the cave'. Holotype NNNU230611, 41.2 mm standard length (text; Table 1 prints 41.7), China: Guangxi, Wuming County, Chuanqian Village, 23°13'25.08"N, 108°26'18.50"E, collected by H.L. Mo and J.H. Zhong in June 2023. Paratypes NNNU230603–230610, 8 ex., 26.1–33.4 mm standard length; same data as for holotype. The Description opens 'The morphometric data of the type specimen of Paranemachilus luegvetensis sp. nov. are given in Table 1.' but does not say which specimens the eye range covers. Table 1 ('Morphometric characters of Paranemachilus luegvetensis sp. nov. and Paranemachilus liui sp. nov.'; columns 'Holotype' and 'Paratypes (n = 8)' for each species; the only unit printed is in the row label 'Standard length/mm') has no eye-diameter, orbital or interorbital row; the rows containing 'eye' are 'Head height at eye' and 'Head width at eye' (luegvetensis: 'Head height at eye' holotype 5.1, paratypes 2.0–4.1 (3.0 ± 0.6); 'Head width at eye' 6.4, 3.2–4.8 (4.1 ± 0.5); 'Head length' 9.7, 7.2–8.7 (8.1 ± 0.6)), so the eye range cannot be checked against the table. Description sentence order as printed: body sentences, 'Mouth inferior, snout obtuse, lips developed ...', the nostril sentence ('Anterior and posterior nostrils adjacent; anterior nostrils tube-like, ...'), the eye sentence, then 'Three pairs of barbels: inner rostral barbel extending to posterior margin of eye, ...'. The Diagnosis has no sentence containing 'eye' or 'orbit'; no sentence compares eye size between species. Discussion (general, no species figure): 'As noted in Ma et al. (2019), cavefish typically possess morphological adaptations to the extreme conditions of cave environments, such as eye degeneration or loss, reduced pigmentation, and diminished scales.' The other species in the paper, P. liui, has 17.3%–21.9% (filed separately).

Description sentence order as printed: body sentences, the nostril sentence ('Anterior and posterior nostrils adjacent; anterior nostrils tube-like; ...'), the eye sentence, then 'Mouth inferior, snout obtuse, lips developed and smooth; in most specimens, median of lower lip with V-shaped notch; missing in specimens such as NNNU230710006 (holotype).', then 'Three pairs of barbels: inner rostral extending to posterior margin of posterior opercular, outer rostral, and maxillary barbel reaching or exceeding posterior margin of head.' (no eye mention). The Diagnosis contains no 'eye' sentence; it prints '11–15 supraorbital canal pores at base of anterior nostrils' (head canal pores, not an eye measure); no sentence compares eye size between species. Discussion (general, no species figure): 'As noted in Ma et al. (2019), cavefish typically possess morphological adaptations to the extreme conditions of cave environments, such as eye degeneration or loss, reduced pigmentation, and diminished scales.' The other species in the paper, P. luegvetensis, has 19.3%–25.3% (filed separately).
